column11: [Plays "Rhythm-a-ning" by Art Pepper, from Gettin' Together, Contemporary Records (1960). Personnel: Art Pepper: alto saxophone; Conte Candoli: trumpet; Wynton Kelly: piano; Paul Chambers: bass; Jimmy Cobb: drums.]
column40: [Plays "Bluesology" by Marvin Jenkins, from Marv Jenkins Arrives, Orovox Records (1961). Personnel: Marvin Jenkins: piano; Milt Jackson: composer.]
column101: [Plays "Our Love Is Here To Stay" by Roland Kirk, from Introducing Roland Kirk, Argo Records (1960). Personnel: Roland Kirk: manzello; William Burton: piano; Don Garrett: bass; Sonny Brown: drums.]

column1: Blindfold Test, with Leonard Feather. Today's guest, Les McCann.
column2: Once again, greetings and modulations. It's our pleasure to bring to you, today, another in a series of interviews designed not only for KNOB, but for future use in DownBeat Magazine.
column3: Today, our guest is a gentleman who has caused quite a little controversy in the music world in the last year, who has a style of jazz that might be described as new or possibly as very old or possibly a combination of the two. Whichever it is, everybody's talking about him, and I'm very proud to introduce Les McCann.
column4: Thank you, Leonard. How are you today?
column5: Pretty good, Les. I'm ready to take off with the first record. I think you probably know the system we've established here.
column7: That is one bell for poor, two bells for fair, three for good, four for very good, and if it's even better than that, you can just push the panic button to indicate that all bells are rung.
column9: We'll go ahead with record number one.
column12: Les McCann can't hear me, but this is the Art Pepper Quintet with Conte Candoli on trumpet playing Thelonious Monk's composition Rhythm-a-Ning.
column13: Well, that was kind of a high tension record in a sense. Kind of makes me nervous in spots. But, I think it was Conte Candoli on trumpet, and probably Art Pepper on alto. But, the part I liked was when the piano player started playing. I think that was the best part.
column15: It could have been Red Garland.
column17: I don't know if that's... I couldn't hardly recognize what it was, but they had a very good feeling there. Kind of that same feeling that The Rhythm Section used to get.
column18: Used to get? You mean under what conditions?
column19: When they were The Rhythm Section. They are not together anymore.
column20: Which rhythm section do you mean?
column21: I meant Philly Joe and Paul Chambers-
column22: Uh-huh. Yeah. I thought that was what you meant. I just wanted-
column25: I give the whole... I didn't like the tune at all.
column30: Well, let's hear rating musically, and...
column31: Okay. For the band, I give it ..., and for the rhythm section ...
column32: All right. Three bells for a Wynton Kelly, Paul Chambers and Jimmy Cobb, that's who was the rhythm section.
column34: You were correct 100% on the front line. It was Art Pepper's date and Conte, of course, on trumpet. The tune is an old Thelonious Monk riff called Rhythm-a-Ning.
column36: It's one of his sillier compositions, I would say. Less vital or more trivial.
column37: It makes me jump when I hear it.
column38: All right, let's jump away from it and move into record number two.
column41: Let's see how Les makes out of this. It's a new pianist by the name of Marv Jenkins on the Orovox Label. The first release on this label, and he's playing Milt Jackson's composition Bluesology.
column42: The tune was Bluesology. I think I heard Bags, or somebody playing that sometime ago.
column43: That's right. In fact, Bags wrote it.
column45: That much I can tell you.
column46: Well, if it's who I think it is, I really want to... I don't think I should completely go on what I feel about it, because this person is a very good friend of mine and...
column48: This is a Marvin Jenkins I think, and I didn't even know he had a record out. I hated the way the whole record was recorded. The sound was horrible. Marvin is one of the few people I knew, who sets a good feeling when he plays and makes everybody happy. I mean this is what I like in music. He plays all the instruments, tenor and a few other things and gets just as, well good a feeling.
column49: What intrigues me is if, let's assume it is Marv Jenkins. I'm not telling you whether it is or not.
column51: What led you to believe it so immediately?
column53: I mean has he as that distinctive of a style?
column56: Yes. That more than any other thing, but he has a way of playing that I can recognize if it's him. If it's somebody else's, that sounded exactly like him.
column58: Well, for Marvin, I give it this ...
column59: Four bells, and it is Marvin Jenkins.
column61: That was very sharp work on your part, because since he hasn't made any records before, as far as I know.
column62: I know he made one record that he doesn't play like this on. It's this Good Little Man, which is a very nice... This is a single that's out with Barney Kessel.
column63: Oh, that's right. He toured with Barney Kessel's group, didn't he?
column67: Yeah, Barney told me about him. As a matter of fact, just around the same time that Gil Fuller brought me this record. This is Gil Fuller's label.
column69: It's a new company, Orovox Records.
column70: I think I would do something about that recording.
column71: Well, maybe so, but there's some interesting playing in there. I'll say that.
column72: There is. Marvin is a very interesting and funniest guy I've ever met in my life.
column73: Is that right? I've got to meet him.
column74: He keeps you laughing all the time.
column75: Would you say he belongs in the so-called groove, funk, soul society?
column76: I think he belongs in the groove happiness society.
column79: I don't want to draw you into a debate necessarily on the subject of this whole thing, except that you are so inextricably associated with it, that it would be almost illogical not to bring it up at one point along the way.
column81: How do you feel in the first place about the identification that you've had with this particular school of music? The neo-gospel style, which of course has been prevalent on quite a number of your performances. Although, not all of it by any means.
column82: Well, I don't mind it, but I just don't want to feel that this is the only way we play. As far as people listening to us, I think that this is our only means of communication, because we play other types of music too. I think that this is not only as me, this goes for a lot of musicians. They play other things, other than one. I mean, maybe not as far as... Well, let me say this now. Not too many groups have been put in a position like we have.
column84: Speaking from us, I think we should be heard from all sides.
column85: That certainly is happening with Horace silver. He was the first, I would say, in the East to be associated with the funk. Matter of fact, you know how it all started? Allegedly, Horace did an arrangement on Show Me the Way to Go Home, or on those changes-
column88: Preacher, yes. Well, see all my life, I haven't heard this kind of music.
column90: So, what are you going to do?
column91: I know it isn't new. That's what I said when I introduced you before. But, the fact is that it's used in this particular context and modern jazz is new.
column92: Well, the reason I want to use it, is because from the feeling that I've heard it throughout the churches and just the groups around the streets that were singing, it was just such a good feeling to me, that if you get this over to the people, I mean you got something going.
column93: I know. I understand your feeling. I think it's a very justifiable objective. It's a funny thing that there has been such a violent reaction for, or against it.
column94: Well, I think a lot of the reaction against me is from... I've heard some musicians talk against us. The fact that I'm so young and...
column95: Yeah, and they accused you of being synthetic with it.
column96: Yeah. We've come out, and fairly successful. Out here, I know there's a feeling of jealousy going on. But, that's all right. I think that as long as we just keep trying to be honest and-
column98: ... being straight with loving everybody, we're going to get our point across.
column99: I'm hip. Let's try record number three.
column102: This one is going to be a surprise to Les. It's a young fellow named Roland Kirk, and he's playing an instrument known as the manzello, on Our Love Is Here To Stay.
column103: Well, the instrument sounded like a soprano saxophone, but I don't know if it was Steve Lacey or a guy I read about. I think he plays about three or four instruments, or something. I'm not sure, but he projected a lot of feeling. At first the rhythm section weren't quite together, but regardless, and despite that he was saying what he had to say right along.
column104: Uh-huh. What do you think of the sound?
column105: Well, I think through him, maybe I could learn to like it, because he seemed to have a lot of control. It was places there, but this is a very hard instrument to play, especially trying to keep it in tune. I don't know if it was a soprano or not, but I liked it, his part.
column106: Well, let's hear the rating and then I'll tell you all about it.
column107: Well, all right. If it wasn't a soprano sax, it was an oboe.
column108: It sure sounded as much like an oboe as it sounded like a soprano. I'll say that.
column112: This is a fellow named Roland Kirk and your guess, your second guess was right. That's a fellow who plays up to three instruments simultaneously.
column114: It's a weird thing. This instrument that he played Love Is Here To Stay on, is called a manzello. It's sort of in the soprano sax family with trumpet and oboe overtones, I would say.
column116: He also plays something called a stritch, S-T-R-I-T-C-H, which is supposed to be like a straight alto saxophone, if you can imagine that. He plays these both at once, and another saxophone-
column118: ... all out of the same mouth. How he does it with only two hands? I'll never figure it out. He is blind, and he is a Chicago musician. This is his first album on the Argo label. I suspect we'll hear a lot more of him. Not because he's a stunt artist that plays three horns at once, but because as you said, what he does, he does with some projection and feeling.
column119: Yeah. See, nowadays it's so hard for a person to come up... so, you say he plays three at once, and right away he's going to be tagged as somebody who's trying to, a fad, you know?
column121: Or, they just tag him with a gimmick. I mean these kind of terms should be thrown out.
column122: There are some tracks on this album, where he does play more than one instruments at once. But, on this particular tune that I chose to play you, he only plays the one of course. I think obviously there's no gimmick attached to this, except that it's an unusual instrument.
column123: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I really liked what he did. I think I should add one more bell to that.
column126: Thank you. Three bells for Roland Kirk. That has nothing to do with your having had the identification given to you after the rating?
column128: All right, thank you. We're talking to Les McCann, and we'll be back with you right after this word from our producer.
column129: One day, this thing will be a reality, but not right now. Not with the scene the way it is. [inaudible], and I thought I had the program pretty well balanced with light things too. There was a lot of that music that was pretentious about the blessed with really great music. But, I was afraid before music, those people shouldn't call absolute music. When I counted, I can't stand them. So, a lot of them, we got to put down a great deal of a lot of the critics because I said...and actually there're just, because nobody can stand unless the guy is a person, is a real connoisseur of music. He cannot stand to sit through a Schoenberg concert, two hours of Schoenberg music, of heavy music.
column130: It's really well. The kind of the fans that you attract to them, probably extending themselves to listen to anything beyond jazz music.
column131: We scared people to death with that orchestra. A lot of the city of class people haven't gotten on that thing.
column132: Yeah, I've played that to people that don't know. I mean on the Blindfold Test basis, and it causes some bewildering reactions.
column135: There's an awful lot of music in Graettinger's things. First of all, there's no tonality whatsoever. It's a complete lost of tonality, and people, it just shows you how much...
column136: It takes a lot of time and a lot of listening.
column137: Sometime back we got to talking about, I wonder what musical sounded like in 500 years. You get excited thinking about what it's going to be like, how if you go to a concert, you will sit in your seat and them perform and you will not to hear any one melody. You'll just hear sheets of musical sound that'll go passing by.
column139: It'll be all shapes [inaudible], because of all the tremendous, complex, contrapuntal things that'll be going on. You'll think you feel this sensation. It'll be like smelling perfume. There's this odor of aroma in that one, and be exciting thing.
column140: That was a very, I thought, fairly intelligent appraisal of City of Blessed by the classical reviewer in DownBeat.
column141: You think so? I don't remember what he said a lot. There's-
column142: Well, it is favorable. But, I mean he reviewed it as if he would be reviewing a regular classical work.
column143: You know where the City of Blessed is appreciated, is in Europe.
column147: Oh no, no. We didn't... See, the difference lying between those people and us Americans over here, is they're more used to these distances and...
column148: Oh, yes. That's true. They're more ready to accept you on the concept level too.
column149: Well that part of it too is in our favor. They don't look at jazz the way we look it over here. Jazz music over here's a thing that goes on down at Eighth Avenue in a honky tonk.
column151: It reflects the life of the honky tonk.
column153: Over there, they don't look at it like that. Jazz is a thing that stands by itself, and it's serious music to the people.
column154: Was it probably the biggest impression you've got on the whole tour? It's had an effect of your tremendous reception. The fact that people were paying such intelligent attention to what you would do.
column155: We played this to awful big crowds of people. Then, you go to talk to them, like it'd be a pin drop thing. Maybe some guy would do grunt or something or make a yell, and the whole audience would go, "Shh".
column156: Yeah. None of that happened in Carnegie Hall.
column159: The greatest problem, the biggest worry I have is that we in America, will start to become bogged down with tradition. So, we're getting out where so much about this country is traditional, and tradition does one thing. It stops progress. It's a real poisonous thing. Not that you have to not respect tradition, but you've got to learn where to be lenient with it.
column161: Oh, yeah. It's not a new balance that's been going on, but I think America is going to be having trouble in another generation or two.
column162: It's having trouble right now. We're in a very reactionary stage of our political and social life and everything else, and that the artistic development has got to be mixed up with that.
column164: I think we got enough here. Let me-
